claim: SMC complexes, such as condensin or cohesin, organize chromatin throughout the cell cycle by a process known as loop extrusion.
source: SMC complexes, such as condensin or cohesin, organize chromatin throughout the cell cycle by a process known as loop extrusion.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that summarizes the general understanding of SMC complex function, supported by the broader literature cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: Modeling assuming two-sided loop extrusion reproduces key features of chromatin organization across different organisms.
source: Modeling assuming two-sided loop extrusion reproduces key features of chromatin organization across different organisms.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to previous modeling studies cited in the introduction and results sections.

claim: In vitro single-molecule experiments confirmed that yeast condensins extrude loops.
source: In vitro single-molecule experiments confirmed that yeast condensins extrude loops, however, they remain anchored to their loading sites and extrude loops in a 'one-sided' manner.
evidence: This claim references experimental observations from single-molecule studies, specifically citing work by Ganji et al., 2018.

claim: Yeast condensins remain anchored to their loading sites and extrude loops in a 'one-sided' manner.
source: In vitro single-molecule experiments confirmed that yeast condensins extrude loops, however, they remain anchored to their loading sites and extrude loops in a 'one-sided' manner.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from Ganji et al., 2018, as cited in the manuscript.

claim: One-sided loop extrusion cannot reproduce mitotic chromosome compaction, interphase domain organization, and bacterial chromosomal arm juxtaposition.
source: While one-sided loop extrusion cannot reproduce these phenomena, variants can recapitulate in vivo observations.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figures 2, 3, and 4.

claim: Variants of one-sided loop extrusion can recapitulate in vivo observations.
source: While one-sided loop extrusion cannot reproduce these phenomena, variants can recapitulate in vivo observations.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations of the switching model, semi-diffusive model, and other variants presented in the results.

claim: SMC complexes in vivo constitute effectively two-sided motors or exhibit biased loading.
source: We predict that SMC complexes in vivo constitute effectively two-sided motors or exhibit biased loading and propose relevant experiments.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results and comparison with experimental data.

claim: Loop extrusion is a viable general mechanism of chromatin organization.
source: Our work suggests that loop extrusion is a viable general mechanism of chromatin organization.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the modeling results showing that certain variants of loop extrusion can explain diverse chromosome organization phenomena.

claim: SMC complexes linearly compact mitotic chromosomes in metazoan cells.
source: SMC complexes linearly compact mitotic chromosomes in metazoan cells (Gibcus et al., 2018; Hirano et al., 1997; Hirano and Mitchison, 1994; Ono et al., 2003; Shintomi et al., 2017; Shintomi et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental studies cited in the text.

claim: SMC complexes maintain topologically associated domains (TADs) in interphase vertebrate cells.
source: maintain topologically associated domains (TADs) in interphase vertebrate cells (Gassler et al., 2017; Haarhuis et al., 2017; Rao et al., 2017; Sanborn et al., 2015; Schwarzer et al., 2017; Wutz et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by multiple Hi-C studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: SMC complexes juxtapose the arms of circular chromosomes in bacteria.
source: and juxtapose the arms of circular chromosomes in bacteria (Marbouty et al., 2015; Tran et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C and other experimental studies in bacteria.

claim: The loop extrusion model posits that a loop-extruding factor (LEF) is comprised of two connected motor subunits that bind to chromatin and form a small chromatin loop.
source: The loop extrusion model posits that a loop-extruding factor (LEF), such as condensin, cohesin, or a bacterial SMC complex (bSMC) is in part comprised of two connected motor subunits that bind to chromatin and form a small chromatin loop by bridging two proximal chromatin segments.
evidence: This is a description of the loop extrusion model as conceptualized in the field.

claim: The SMC complex progressively enlarges the loop by reeling chromatin from outside the loop into the growing loop.
source: The SMC complex progressively enlarges the loop by reeling chromatin from outside the loop into the growing loop (Alipour and Marko, 2012; Nasmyth, 2001; Riggs, 1990).
evidence: This is a description of the loop extrusion mechanism supported by theoretical models.

claim: Two-sided extrusion models recapitulate experimental observations of mitotic chromosome compaction and resolution, interphase TAD and loop formation, and juxtaposition of bacterial chromosome arms.
source: This 'two-sided' extrusion model recapitulates experimental observations of mitotic chromosome compaction and resolution, interphase TAD and loop formation, and juxtaposition of bacterial chromosome arms (Alipour and Marko, 2012; Fudenberg et al., 2016; Goloborodko et al., 2016a; Goloborodko et al., 2016b; Miermans and Broedersz, 2018; Sanborn et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple modeling studies cited in the text.

claim: Yeast, human, and Xenopus condensin and Xenopus cohesin complexes extrude DNA loops in an ATP-dependent, directed manner at speeds on the order of 1 kb/s.
source: Recent in vitro single-molecule experiments have imaged loop extrusion of DNA by individual SMC condensin and cohesin complexes, demonstrating that yeast, human, and Xenopus condensin and Xenopus cohesin complexes extrude DNA loops in an ATP-dependent, directed manner at speeds on the order of 1 kb/s (Davidson et al., 2019; Ganji et al., 2018; Golfier et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2019; Kong et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on direct experimental observations from multiple single-molecule studies.

claim: A significant fraction of both human and Xenopus SMC complexes reel in DNA from only one side.
source: Strikingly, however, yeast condensins (Ganji et al., 2018) and a significant fraction of both human and Xenopus SMC complexes (Golfier et al., 2020; Kong et al., 2020) reel in DNA from only one side, while the other side remains anchored to its DNA loading site.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from single-molecule studies.

claim: Bacterial SMC complexes are directly involved in two-sided loop extrusion in vivo.
source: This contrasts with prior observations in bacteria demonstrating the direct involvement of SMC complexes in two-sided loop extrusion in vivo (Tran et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations in bacteria.

claim: Purely 'one-sided' loop extrusion is intrinsically far less effective in linearly compacting DNA than two-sided extrusion.
source: Furthermore, recent theoretical work shows that purely 'one-sided' loop extrusion, as it has been observed in vitro so far, is intrinsically far less effective in linearly compacting DNA than two-sided extrusion (Banigan and Mirny, 2019).
evidence: This is based on theoretical modeling work.

claim: Electron microscopy reveals that chromatin in mitotic chromosomes is arranged in arrays of loops.
source: In mitotic chromosomes, electron microscopy reveals that chromatin is arranged in arrays of loops (Earnshaw and Laemmli, 1983; Maeshima et al., 2005; Marsden and Laemmli, 1979; Paulson and Laemmli, 1977).
evidence: This is based on electron microscopy studies of mitotic chromosomes.

claim: Mitotic chromosome compaction results in dramatic linear compaction of the chromatin fiber into a polymer brush with a > 100 fold shorter backbone.
source: This results in dramatic linear compaction of the chromatin fiber into a polymer brush with a > 100 fold shorter backbone (Guacci et al., 1994; Lawrence et al., 1988; Trask et al., 1989).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements of chromosome compaction.

claim: Fluorescence imaging and Hi-C show that loops in mitotic chromosomes maintain the linear ordering of the genome.
source: Fluorescence imaging and Hi-C show that these loops maintain the linear ordering of the genome (Gibcus et al., 2018; Naumova et al., 2013; Strukov and Belmont, 2009; Trask et al., 1993).
evidence: This is based on fluorescence imaging and Hi-C studies.

claim: The two-sided loop extrusion model reproduces experimental observations of mitotic chromosome compaction.
source: Each of these experimental observations is reproduced by the two-sided loop extrusion model, in which dynamic loop-extruding condensins collectively form arrays of reinforced loops by locally extruding chromatin until encountering another condensin (Goloborodko et al., 2016a; Goloborodko et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is based on modeling studies that reproduce experimental observations.

claim: One-sided loop extrusion can only linearly compact chromosomes 10-fold because it leaves unlooped polymer gaps between loop extruders.
source: The simplest one-sided loop extrusion process, in contrast, can only linearly compact chromosomes 10-fold because it leaves unlooped (and thus, uncompacted) polymer gaps between loop extruders (Banigan and Mirny, 2019
evidence: This is based on theoretical modeling work.

claim: Variants of one-sided loop extrusion in which loop extruders are effectively two-sided may robustly compact mitotic chromosomes.
source: Nonetheless, variants of one-sided loop extrusion in which loop extruders are effectively two-sided may robustly compact mitotic chromosomes (Banigan and Mirny, 2019).
evidence: This is based on theoretical modeling work.

claim: In interphase in vertebrate cells, the SMC cohesin complex is responsible for frequent but transient loop formation, which results in regions of high intra-chromatin contact frequency referred to as TADs.
source: In interphase in vertebrate cells, Hi-C reveals that the SMC cohesin complex is responsible for frequent but transient loop formation, which results in regions of high intra-chromatin contact frequency referred to as TADs (Dixon et al., 2012; Gassler et al., 2017; Haarhuis et al., 2017; Nora et al., 2012; Rao et al., 2017; Rao et al., 2014; Schwarzer et al., 2017; Sexton et al., 2012; Sofueva et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on Hi-C studies of interphase chromosomes.

claim: TADs are bordered by convergently oriented CTCF protein binding sites.
source: These regions are bordered by convergently oriented CTCF protein binding sites (de Wit et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2015; Rao et al., 2014; Sanborn et al., 2015; Vietri Rudan et al., 2015)
evidence: This is based on Hi-C and ChIP-seq studies.

claim: CTCF binding sites act as obstacles to loop extrusion and translocation of cohesin.
source: which act as obstacles to loop extrusion and translocation of cohesin (Busslinger et al., 2017; de Wit et al., 2015; Fudenberg et al., 2016; Nora et al., 2017; Sanborn et al., 2015; Wutz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on experimental and modeling studies.

claim: The two-sided loop extrusion model explains the emergence of TADs and their 'corner peaks' and 'stripes' in Hi-C maps.
source: The two-sided loop extrusion model explains the emergence of TADs and their 'corner peaks' (or 'dots') and 'stripes' (sometimes called 'lines', 'tracks' or 'flames') in Hi-C maps as an average collective effect of multiple cohesins dynamically extruding chromatin loops and stopping at the CTCF boundaries (Fudenberg et al., 2016; Sanborn et al., 2015; reviewed in Fudenberg et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on modeling studies that reproduce Hi-C patterns.

claim: A one-sided LEF will necessarily leave an unlooped gap between its initial loading site and one of the CTCF boundary elements.
source: While it is clear that a one-sided LEF will necessarily leave an unlooped gap between its initial loading site and one of the CTCF boundary elements, the extent to which one-sided loop extrusion can recapitulate the experimental observations remains entirely unexplored.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the one-sided extrusion mechanism.

claim: In Bacillus subtilis and Caulobacter crescentus, the circular chromosome exhibits enhanced contact frequency between its two chromosomal arms.
source: In Bacillus subtilis and Caulobacter crescentus, the circular chromosome exhibits enhanced contact frequency between its two chromosomal arms (often called 'replichores'), as shown by Hi-C (Le et al., 2013; Marbouty et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on Hi-C studies in bacteria.

claim: The enhanced contact frequency between bacterial chromosome arms is dependent on the bacterial SMC complex (bSMC).
source: This signal is dependent on the bacterial SMC complex (bSMC) (Marbouty et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on experimental studies in bacteria.

claim: bSMC is loaded at a bacterial parS site near the origin of replication, and then actively and processively moves along the chromosome, juxtaposing the arms together.
source: Experiments show that bSMC is loaded at a bacterial parS site near the origin of replication, and then, while bridging the two arms, actively and processively moves along the chromosome, thus juxtaposing or 'zipping' the arms together (Minnen et al., 2016; Tran et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on experimental studies in bacteria.

claim: The symmetry of the juxtaposed chromosome arms implies that bSMC should be a two-sided LEF.
source: The symmetry of the juxtaposed chromosome arms implies that bSMC should be a two-sided LEF (Brandão et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the symmetry observed in Hi-C maps and supported by modeling studies.

claim: Pure one-sided loop extrusion produces contact maps that differ from experimental observations in bacteria.
source: Indeed, previous modeling has shown that pure one-sided loop extrusion produces contact maps that differ from experimental observations (Miermans and Broedersz, 2018).
evidence: This is based on modeling studies.

claim: Pure one-sided loop extrusion fails to capture most of the in vivo phenomenology of chromosome organization.
source: By comparing our results to experimental data, we find that pure one-sided loop extrusion fails to capture most of the in vivo phenomenology.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Simple variants of the one-sided model that make loop extrusion effectively two-sided or otherwise suppress the formation of unlooped chromatin gaps can restore the emergent features of chromatin organization observed in experiments.
source: However, simple variants of the one-sided model that make loop extrusion effectively two-sided or otherwise suppress the formation of unlooped chromatin gaps can restore the emergent features of chromatin organization observed in experiments.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations of various model variants.

claim: In the loop extrusion model, a LEF is comprised of two subunits, which can either be active or inactive.
source: In our model, loop extrusion is performed by loop-extruding factors (LEFs), which may be a single SMC complex, a dimer of SMC complexes, or any other oligomer of SMC complexes. A LEF is comprised of two subunits, which can either be active or inactive.
evidence: This is a description of the model used in the simulations.

claim: Each active subunit can processively translocate along the chromatin fiber, thus creating and enlarging the chromatin loop between the subunits.
source: Each active subunit can processively translocate along the chromatin fiber, thus creating and enlarging the chromatin (or DNA) loop between the subunits (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism, illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: An inactive subunit can either be anchored or passively slide/diffuse along the fiber, depending on the specific model.
source: An inactive subunit can either be anchored or passively slide/diffuse along the fiber, depending on the specific model (see below).
evidence: This is a description of the different model variants explored in the study.

claim: Two-sided LEFs have two active subunits that on average grow a chromatin loop by translocating in opposing directions.
source: In existing simulation models of loop extrusion (Alipour and Marko, 2012; Brandão et al., 2019; Fudenberg et al., 2016; Goloborodko et al., 2016a; Goloborodko et al., 2016b; Miermans and Broedersz, 2018; Sanborn et al., 2015), LEFs are 'two-sided,' that is they have two active subunits that on average grow a chromatin loop by translocating in opposing directions (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a description of the two-sided extrusion model, illustrated in Figure 1b.

claim: One-sided LEFs have one active subunit and one inactive (passive) subunit.
source: Here, we consider 'one-sided' LEFs that have one active subunit and one inactive (passive) subunit.
evidence: This is a description of the one-sided extrusion model explored in the study.

claim: LEFs bind to chromatin with association rate kbind and unbind from chromatin with dissociation rate kunbind.
source: In our model, LEFs bind to chromatin with association rate kbind and unbind from chromatin with dissociation rate kunbind (mean residence time τ = 1/kunbind).
evidence: This is a description of the model parameters.

claim: A LEF's active subunit translocates at speed v along the chromosome, away from its passive subunit, thus growing the chromatin loop.
source: A LEF's active subunit translocates at speed v along the chromosome, away from its passive subunit, thus growing the chromatin loop.
evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism.

claim: LEF subunits cannot translocate through other LEF subunits unless otherwise stated.
source: Furthermore, LEF subunits cannot translocate through other LEF subunits unless otherwise stated; extrusion by an active LEF subunit halts when it encounters another LEF subunit.
evidence: This is a description of a constraint in the model.

claim: The pure one-sided and two-sided loop-extrusion models are primarily controlled by two length scales, λ and d.
source: The pure one-sided and two-sided loop-extrusion models are primarily controlled by two length scales, λ and d (Banigan and Mirny, 2019; Fudenberg et al., 2016; Goloborodko et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is a description of the key parameters in the model, supported by previous theoretical work.

claim: The LEF processivity λ is given by λ = qv/kunbind, where q = 1 or q = 2 for one- and two-sided, respectively.
source: The LEF processivity λ is given by λ = qv/kunbind, where q = 1 or q = 2 for one- and two-sided, respectively
evidence: This is a definition of the processivity parameter in the model.

claim: One-sided LEFs with extrusion velocity v grow loops at half the speed of two-sided LEFs with the same v.
source: thus, one-sided LEFs with extrusion velocity v grow loops at half the speed of two-sided LEFs with the same v (see arch diagrams in Figure 1b and c, bottom).
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the model definition, illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: d = L/Nb is the mean distance between the Nb LEFs bound to the fiber of length L.
source: d = L/Nb, is the mean distance between the Nb LEFs bound to the fiber of length L (where Nb = N kbind/(kbind+kunbind)).
evidence: This is a definition of the mean distance parameter in the model.

claim: For λ <d, LEFs are sparse and on average do not meet.
source: For λ <d, LEFs are sparse and on average do not meet.
evidence: This is a description of the model behavior in a specific parameter regime.

claim: For λ >d, LEFs are densely loaded on the chromatin, and a translocating LEF typically encounters other LEFs.
source: For λ >d, LEFs are densely loaded on the chromatin, and a translocating LEF typically encounters other LEFs.
evidence: This is a description of the model behavior in a specific parameter regime.

claim: In pure one-sided loop extrusion, the passive subunit of the bound LEF remains stationary on the chromatin fiber for the entire residence time of the LEF.
source: In pure one-sided loop extrusion, the passive subunit of the bound LEF remains stationary on the chromatin fiber for the entire residence time of the LEF, while the active subunit translocates at speed v away from the passive subunit.
evidence: This is a description of the pure one-sided extrusion model.

claim: LEFs bind with a random orientation in the pure one-sided extrusion model.
source: LEFs bind with a random orientation.
evidence: This is a description of the model assumption.

claim: Individual LEFs asymmetrically extrude loops in the pure one-sided extrusion model, as observed in Ganji et al. (2018).
source: Individual LEFs asymmetrically extrude loops, as observed in Ganji et al. (2018).
evidence: This is a description of the model behavior, consistent with experimental observations.

claim: In the semi-diffusive model, the active LEF subunit translocates at speed v, while the inactive LEF subunit stochastically diffuses along the fiber.
source: We also considered a model in which the active LEF subunit translocates at speed v, while the inactive LEF subunit stochastically diffuses (slides) along the fiber.
evidence: This is a description of the semi-diffusive model.

claim: The semi-diffusive model is motivated by the experimental observation of the yeast condensin 'safety belt'.
source: This model is primarily motivated by the experimental observation of the yeast condensin 'safety belt' (Kschonsak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a description of the motivation for the semi-diffusive model.

claim: The condensin 'safety belt' is thought to anchor the LEF in place as it extrudes loops in a one-sided manner, but the safety belt can be released via protein alterations, allowing the passive subunit of the SMC complex to diffuse along DNA.
source: This condensin component is thought to anchor the LEF in place as it extrudes loops in a one-sided manner, but the safety belt can be released via protein alterations, allowing the passive subunit of the SMC complex to diffuse along DNA (Ganji et al., 2018; Kschonsak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental basis for the semi-diffusive model.

claim: Several in vitro experiments have imaged cohesins and condensins diffusively translocating along naked DNA with diffusion coefficients of D = 0.001–4 μm2/s.
source: In addition, we note that several in vitro experiments have imaged cohesins and condensins diffusively translocating along naked DNA with diffusion coefficients of D = 0.001–4 μm2/s (or D = 0.01–35 kb2/s) (Davidson et al., 2016; Kanke et al., 2016; Kim and Loparo, 2016; Kim et al., 2019; Stigler et al., 2016; Terakawa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements of SMC complex diffusion.

claim: In the semi-diffusive model, the inactive subunit stochastically translocates by taking diffusive steps in either direction, with the stepping rate modulated by the entropic penalty for polymer loop formation.
source: In the model, the inactive subunit stochastically translocates by taking diffusive steps in either direction. The stepping rate in each direction is modulated by the entropic penalty for polymer loop formation (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the semi-diffusive model mechanism.

claim: In the semi-diffusive model, the sliding tends to shrink small loops, while having little effect on large loops.
source: As a result of this effect, the sliding tends to shrink small loops, while having little effect on large loops.
evidence: This is a description of the model behavior.

claim: In the switching model, LEFs are instantaneously one-sided but stochastically switch which subunit actively translocates.
source: As another alternative model, we consider a scenario in which LEFs are instantaneously one-sided (i.e., one subunit is active and the other is inactive and stationary), but stochastically switch which subunit actively translocates.
evidence: This is a description of the switching model.

claim: The switching model captures the dynamics of a proposed mechanism dubbed 'asymmetric strand switching'.
source: This model captures the dynamics of a proposed mechanism dubbed 'asymmetric strand switching' (see Figure 2d in Hassler et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a description of the motivation for the switching model.

claim: Switching could be achieved through a stochastic segment/loop-capture mechanism.
source: As described in Marko et al. (2019), switching could be achieved through a stochastic segment/loop-capture mechanism.
evidence: This is a description of a possible molecular mechanism for switching.

claim: In the switching model, switches occur at rate kswitch.
source: In our model, switches occur at rate kswitch; by switching, inactive subunits become active and vice versa.
evidence: This is a description of the switching model parameter.

claim: Switching activity of SMC complexes could potentially be induced by exchange of subunits within the SMC complex, different solution conditions, or post-translational or genetic modifications.
source: Although not yet observed experimentally, we hypothesize that switching activity of SMC complexes could potentially be induced by exchange of subunits within the SMC complex, different solution conditions, or post-translational or genetic modifications, all of which can alter SMC complex behavior in experiments (Eeftens et al., 2017; Elbatsh et al., 2019; Ganji et al., 2018; Keenholtz et al., 2017; Kleine Borgmann et al., 2013; Kschonsak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about possible mechanisms for inducing switching, supported by experimental observations of factors that alter SMC behavior.

claim: For kswitch/kunbind <1, switches rarely occur and LEF trajectories typically appear to be pure one-sided.
source: For kswitch/kunbind <1, switches rarely occur and LEF trajectories typically appear to be pure one-sided.
evidence: This is a description of the model behavior in a specific parameter regime.

claim: For kswitch/kunbind >1, the active and inactive LEF subunits may frequently switch before unbinding chromatin.
source: In contrast, for kswitch/kunbind >1, the active and inactive LEF subunits may frequently switch before unbinding chromatin, and trajectories appear as in Figure 1e, top panel.
evidence: This is a description of the model behavior in a specific parameter regime, illustrated in Figure 1e.

claim: 3D polymer simulations were performed using molecular dynamics simulations using OpenMM.
source: To do this, we coupled each of the 1D loop-extrusion models in Figure 1 to a 3D model of a polymer chain (Fudenberg et al., 2016; Goloborodko et al., 2016a) and performed molecular dynamics simulations using OpenMM (see Materials and methods for details) (Eastman et al., 2017; Eastman et al., 2013; Eastman and Pande, 2010).
evidence: This is a description of the simulation method used.

claim: In the coupled model, LEFs act as a bond between the two sites (monomers) to which the LEF subunits are bound.
source: In this coupled model, LEFs act as a bond between the two sites (monomers) to which the LEF subunits are bound; these bonds have the dynamics described for LEFs above.
evidence: This is a description of how LEFs are modeled in the 3D polymer simulations.

claim: Contact maps were generated semi-analytically from the 1D models of the underlying SMC dynamics.
source: In addition to 3D polymer simulations, we generated contact maps semi-analytically from the 1D models of the underlying SMC dynamics.
evidence: This is a description of an alternative method for generating contact maps.

claim: The semi-analytical method allowed exploration of a broad range of parameter values and assessment of the resulting Hi-C-like maps in a computationally inexpensive manner.
source: This method allowed us to explore a broad range of parameter values and assess the resulting Hi-C-like maps in a computationally inexpensive manner.
evidence: This is a description of the advantage of the semi-analytical method.

claim: The semi-analytical method is not used for modeling the eukaryotic systems because the Gaussian approximation used is not appropriate for highly compacted mitotic and 'vermicelli' interphase chromosomes.
source: The semi-analytical method is not used for modeling the eukaryotic systems because the Gaussian approximation used is not appropriate for highly compacted mitotic and 'vermicelli' (i.e., Wapl depletion [Tedeschi et al., 2013]) interphase chromosomes, which have linearly dense arrays of chromatin loops.
evidence: This is a description of the limitation of the semi-analytical method.

claim: The two-sided loop extrusion model can rapidly achieve 1000-fold linear compaction in the regime in which LEFs are densely loaded on the chromosome (λ/d≳10).
source: Previous work suggests that the two-sided loop extrusion model can rapidly achieve 1000-fold linear compaction in the regime in which LEFs are densely loaded on the chromosome (λ/d≳10), which is expected for mitotic chromosomes in metazoan cells (Goloborodko et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is based on previous modeling work.

claim: With a loop extrusion speed of v≈1 kb/s, two-sided extrusion can achieve full linear compaction within one residence time (1/kunbind ~ 2–10 min).
source: With a loop extrusion speed of v≈1 kb/s (Ganji et al., 2018), two-sided extrusion can achieve full linear compaction within one residence time (1/kunbind ~ 2–10 min [Gerlich et al., 2006a; Terakawa et al., 2017; Walther et al., 2018])
evidence: This is based on modeling work and experimental measurements of extrusion speed and residence time.

claim: Full 3D compaction and loop maturation occurs over a few (<10) residence times in the two-sided extrusion model.
source: and full 3D compaction and loop maturation occurs over a few (<10) residence times (Goloborodko et al., 2016a), consistent with the duration of prophase and prometaphase and in vivo observations of mitotic chromosome compaction (Eykelenboom et al., 2019; Gibcus et al., 2018) and resolution (Eykelenboom et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on modeling work and experimental observations.

claim: Pure one-sided loop extrusion cannot linearly compact a chromatin fiber by more than ~10 fold.
source: In contrast, theoretical work has demonstrated that pure one-sided loop extrusion cannot linearly compact a chromatin fiber by more than ~10 fold (Banigan and Mirny, 2019).
evidence: This is based on theoretical modeling work.

claim: Linear compaction in loop extrusion models depends only on the dimensionless ratio of length scales λ/d.
source: Linear compaction in these models depends only on the dimensionless ratio of length scales λ/d (Banigan and Mirny, 2019; Goloborodko et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is based on theoretical modeling work.

claim: The compacted fraction, f, is defined as the fraction of chromosome length that is contained within looped regions.
source: To measure linear compaction, we define the compacted fraction, f, as the fraction of chromosome length that is contained within looped regions and the resulting linear fold compaction as FC = 1/(1-f).
evidence: This is a definition of a metric used in the study.

claim: The resulting linear fold compaction is FC = 1/(1-f).
source: To measure linear compaction, we define the compacted fraction, f, as the fraction of chromosome length that is contained within looped regions and the resulting linear fold compaction as FC = 1/(1-f).
evidence: This is a definition of a metric used in the study.

claim: Chromosome volume, V, is expected to decrease by >2 fold during mitotic compaction.
source: We measure the resulting 3D compaction by computing chromosome volume, V, which is expected to decrease by >2 fold during mitotic compaction (Daban, 2003; Hihara et al., 2012; Liang et al., 2015; Nagasaka et al., 2016; Sumner, 1991).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements of chromosome volume during mitosis.

claim: Chromatid resolution is quantified by measuring the median inter-chromatid backbone distance, ΔR, scaled by the polymer backbone length, Rb.
source: We quantify chromatid resolution by measuring the median inter-chromatid backbone distance, ΔR, scaled by the polymer backbone length, Rb.
evidence: This is a description of a metric used in the study.

claim: Larger distances, ΔR/Rb >1, indicates that typical inter-chromatid distances are sufficient to prevent contacts between backbones.
source: Larger distances, ΔR/Rb >1, indicates that typical inter-chromatid distances are sufficient to prevent contacts between backbones.
evidence: This is a description of the interpretation of the metric.

claim: Larger median distance and smaller overlap are expected to contribute to the disentanglement of chromatids.
source: Larger median distance and smaller overlap are expected to contribute to the disentanglement of chromatids (Piskadlo et al., 2017; Sen et al., 2016), which facilitates chromosome segregation by preventing anaphase bridge formation (Charbin et al., 2014; Green et al., 2012; Hagstrom et al., 2002; Nagasaka et al., 2016; Piskadlo et al., 2017; Steffensen et al., 2001).
evidence: This is based on experimental and theoretical work on chromosome segregation.

claim: Pure one-sided loop extrusion saturates at ≈10-fold compaction for large λ/d, as predicted by mean-field theory.
source: Figure 2c (i) shows linear fold compaction, FC, as a function of λ/d in the simulations, and results for λ/d>>1 are consistent with the theoretical predictions (Banigan and Mirny, 2019).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 2c(i) and comparison with theory.

claim: The compaction limit in pure one-sided extrusion is due to the unavoidable presence of 'gaps' of uncompacted (unlooped) chromatin between some adjacent loops.
source: The compaction limit is due to the unavoidable presence of 'gaps' of uncompacted (unlooped) chromatin between some adjacent loops (Figure 2c (ii))
evidence: This is explained by the model mechanism and illustrated in Figure 2c(ii).

claim: Of the four possible orientations of adjacent translocating LEFs, →→, ←←, →←, and ←→, the last one necessarily leaves an unlooped gap.

claim: In pure one-sided loop extrusion, one LEF subunit is fixed at the parS loading site, while the other subunit translocates away from it.

claim: One-sided extrusion with directional switching can juxtapose chromosome arms if the switching rate is fast enough (kswitchL/v > 200).

claim: For B. subtilis and C. crescentus, the upper bound on the mean time between switches is approximately 2–10 s and 10–20 s, respectively.

claim: One-sided extrusion with switching can juxtapose chromosomal arms, as demonstrated by the presence of the Hi-C secondary diagonal.

evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: In the switching model, a relatively fast switching rate is required, which effectively makes a one-sided LEF behave like a two-sided LEF at the physiologically relevant time scales of a few minutes.
source: In our model, this requires a relatively fast switching rate, which effectively makes a one-sided LEF behave like a two-sided LEF at the physiologically relevant time scales of a few minutes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulation results.

source: Other variants of one-sided mechanism cannot achieve juxtaposition of bacterial arms due to tethers that remain between distal chromosome loci and the LEF loading site, indicating that bSMC is an effectively two-sided extruder.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results and comparison with previous theoretical work.

claim: Recent experimental evidence suggests that pairs of yeast condensins may be able to cooperatively grow loops bidirectionally.
source: Indeed, recent experimental evidence suggests that pairs of yeast condensins may be able to cooperatively grow loops bidirectionally (Kim et al., 2020)
evidence: This is based on recent experimental observations.

claim: Human and Xenopus condensins and cohesins can perform either one- or two-sided loop extrusion.
source: while human and Xenopus condensins and cohesins can perform either one- or two-sided loop extrusion (Davidson et al., 2019; Golfier et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2019; Kong et al., 2020; Moevus, 2019).
evidence: This is based on recent experimental observations.

claim: The ability to robustly eliminate unlooped gaps is essential to the chromosome-organizing role of LEFs.
source: Our modeling demonstrates that the ability to robustly eliminate unlooped gaps is essential to the chromosome-organizing role of LEFs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: Models in which gaps persist in steady state, such as the pure one-sided model, fail to reproduce hallmarks of chromosome organization found in several physiological scenarios.
source: As a result, models in which gaps persist in steady state, such as the pure one-sided model, fail to reproduce hallmarks of chromosome organization found in several physiological scenarios.

source: Importantly, even dynamic LEF turnover (i.e., allowing dynamic chromatin unbinding with uniform rebinding) does not eliminate gaps because LEF unbinding (and even LEF binding) can introduce new gaps.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the model mechanism.

claim: Chromosome compaction, resolution, and interphase organization can readily be explained by physical mechanisms that either eliminate gaps by turning one-sided extrusion into effectively two-sided extrusion or suppress the creation of gaps.
source: Instead, chromosome compaction, resolution, and interphase organization can readily be explained by physical mechanisms that either eliminate gaps by turning one-sided extrusion into effectively two-sided extrusion (e.g., as in the switching model) or suppress the creation of gaps (e.g., by biased loading at boundaries).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: Linear compaction by pure one-sided loop extrusion is limited to ~10 fold because it unavoidably leaves gaps between SMC complexes.
source: In the case of mitotic chromosome compaction, linear compaction by pure one-sided loop extrusion is limited to ~10 fold because it unavoidably leaves gaps between SMC complexes (Figure 2c (i), (ii) and [Banigan and Mirny, 2019]).

claim: 10-fold linear compaction is not sufficient to reproduce the classical 3D shapes of mitotic chromatids and chromosomes are volumetrically compacted at most twofold in 3D.

claim: This defect in 3D compaction leads to defects in mitotic chromosome resolution.
source: This defect in 3D compaction leads to defects in mitotic chromosome resolution (Figure 2 b,c (iv)).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 2.

claim: Allowing the SMC complexes' anchor points to diffuse along chromosomes does not close gaps because loop formation is opposed by the conformational entropy of the formed loop.
source: Allowing the SMC complexes' anchor points to diffuse (i.e., slide) along chromosomes also does not close gaps because loop formation is opposed by the conformational entropy of the formed loop (Figure 2d (ii) and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The LEFs cannot generate a sufficient increase in linear compaction for any diffusive stepping rate, vdiff.
source: Therefore, the LEFs cannot generate a sufficient increase in linear compaction for any diffusive stepping rate, vdiff (or diffusion coefficient, D) (Figure 2d (i))
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 2d(i).

source: in vitro experiments also show that one-sided condensins with diffusing safety belts do not grow large DNA loops (Ganji et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: With one-sided LEFs, uncompacted gaps are pervasive, so simply adding a small fraction of two-sided LEFs is unable to sufficiently compact chromosomes.
source: More generally, with one-sided LEFs, uncompacted gaps are pervasive, so simply adding a small fraction of two-sided LEFs is unable to sufficiently compact chromosomes; in vivo levels of compaction requires >80% two-sided LEFs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Banigan and Mirny, 2019).

claim: A model in which LEFs are effectively two-sided, such as the switching model, can generate greater than twofold 3D compaction and clear resolution of sister chromatids.
source: Similarly, a model in which LEFs are effectively two-sided, such as the switching model in which the active and inactive subunits dynamically switch, can generate greater than twofold 3D compaction and clear resolution of sister chromatids (Figure 2e (iii), (iv)), as observed in vivo.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Such a switching mechanism could be achieved in vivo by a stochastic strand switching mechanism in which both upstream and downstream DNA can be captured by the loop extruder.
source: Such a switching mechanism could be achieved in vivo by a stochastic strand switching mechanism in which both upstream and downstream DNA can be captured by the loop extruder (Hassler et al., 2018; Marko et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about a possible molecular mechanism, supported by theoretical work.

claim: One-sided extrusion with uniform association and dissociation of LEFs can generate TADs and 'stripes' on Hi-C maps.
source: We found that one-sided extrusion with uniform association and dissociation of LEFs can generate TADs (Figure 3b, right) and 'stripes' (or 'flames,' 'tracks,' or 'lines') (Fudenberg et al., 2017; Fudenberg et al., 2016; Vian et al., 2018) on Hi-C maps (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 3b.

claim: One-sided extrusion cannot reliably bring CTCF barriers together, and thus, cannot generate the dots (corner peaks) that are prominent features of Hi-C and micro-C maps.
source: However, one-sided extrusion cannot reliably bring CTCF barriers together, and thus, cannot generate the dots (corner peaks) that are prominent features of Hi-C and micro-C maps (Krietenstein et al., 2020) and are reproduced by two-sided extrusion (Figure 3b, right and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The presence of unavoidable gaps between LEFs and between LEFs and barriers is the reason for the deficiency in generating dots.
source: The presence of unavoidable gaps between LEFs and between LEFs and barriers is the reason for this deficiency.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the model mechanism.

source: This can be remedied by introducing a comparable number of two-sided LEFs to close gaps (Figure 3d, right).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 3d.

claim: One-sided extrusion alone can reproduce dots when undergoing frequent stochastic switches in translocation direction, turning one-sided into effectively two-sided extrusion.
source: One-sided extrusion alone, however, can reproduce dots when undergoing frequent stochastic switches in translocation direction, turning one-sided into effectively two-sided extrusion.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results.

claim: Another strategy to eliminate gaps between boundaries and generate dots is to have strongly (>100 fold) biased loading of LEFs at barriers.
source: Another strategy to eliminate gaps between boundaries and generate dots is to have strongly (>100 fold) biased loading of LEFs at barriers.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results.

claim: Loading of cohesin at CTCF sites has been proposed since the two were found to colocalize.
source: Loading of cohesin at CTCF sites has been proposed since the two were found to colocalize (Nichols and Corces, 2015; Rubio et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

source: Available experimental evidence, however, argues against loading at CTCF sites; it was previously shown that CTCF is dispensable for cohesin loading (Parelho et al., 2008; Wendt et al., 2008)
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: CTCF-degradation experiments appear to have little effect on the levels of chromatin-associated cohesin.
source: and more recently, CTCF-degradation experiments appear to have little effect on the levels of chromatin-associated cohesin (Busslinger et al., 2017; Nora et al., 2019; Nora et al., 2017) and the extent of loop extrusion (Fudenberg et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

source: The challenge for one-sided loop extrusion models in bacteria is to explain how one-sided (i.e., asymmetric) LEF translocation might generate symmetrically aligned contacts between chromosome arms.
evidence: This is a description of the challenge addressed by the modeling.

claim: Allowing diffusion of the anchor point does not help because this type of asymmetric extrusion cannot promote symmetric juxtaposition of the chromosome arms.
source: Furthermore, we find that allowing diffusion of the anchor point does not help because this type of asymmetric extrusion cannot promote symmetric juxtaposition of the chromosome arms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: The switching model, with a switching time on the order of seconds, exhibits the desired effectively two-sided property and naturally creates the desired symmetry of contacts between left and right chromosome arms.
source: The switching model, however, with a switching time on the order of seconds (<10 s for B. subtilis and <20 s for C. crescentus, i.e., rates kswitch≳0.1 s−1; Figure 4d) exhibits the desired effectively two-sided property and naturally creates the desired symmetry of contacts between left and right chromosome arms.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 4d.

claim: If bSMCs function by one-sided extrusion with switching, this constraint suggests that bSMCs can switch their direction of extrusion within a few ATPase cycles.
source: Interestingly, if bSMCs function by one-sided extrusion with switching, this constraint suggests that bSMCs can switch their direction of extrusion within a few ATPase cycles (the B. subtilis SMC complex has an ATPase rate of 0.7 ATP/s [Wang et al., 2018]).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the simulation results and experimental measurements of ATPase rate.

claim: Switching has not been observed in single-molecule experiments with yeast condensin SMC complexes.
source: Switching, however, has not been observed in single-molecule experiments with yeast condensin SMC complexes, and such fast switching may appear as two-sided extrusion in vitro.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of experimental observations.

claim: It was recently suggested that B. subtilis SMCs have two independent motor activities for extrusion.
source: We note that it was recently suggested that B. subtilis SMCs have two independent motor activities for extrusion (Brandão et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2017); this observation is consistent with either two-sided extrusion or one-sided extrusion with rapid switching.
evidence: This is based on recent experimental observations.

claim: Microscopically one-sided extrusion can explain juxtaposition of chromosome arms, provided that bSMCs act as effectively two-sided extruders.
source: Thus, our model suggests that microscopically one-sided extrusion can explain juxtaposition of chromosome arms, provided that bSMCs act as effectively two-sided extruders.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: The ~10 fold linear compaction achievable by pure one-sided loop extrusion is consistent with fluorescence in situ hybridization imaging of yeast mitotic chromosomes.
source: The ~10 fold linear compaction achievable by pure one-sided loop extrusion is consistent with fluorescence in situ hybridization imaging of yeast mitotic chromosomes (Guacci et al., 1994; Kruitwagen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on comparison of simulation results with experimental measurements.

source: Moreover, previous modeling of budding yeast mitotic chromosomes indicated that just ~30–40% coverage by cohesin-extruded loops (i.e.,~2 fold linear compaction, Figure 2—figure supplement 7) produces chromosome contact maps consistent with those obtained from Hi-C experiments (Schalbetter et al., 2017).

source: This lesser degree of compaction generally leads to poorly resolved sister chromatids in our model (Figure 2b,c (iii), and c (iv)), but chromatid resolution in yeast could be facilitated by spindle tension (Lazar‐Stefanita et al., 2017) and the shorter length of yeast chromosomes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulation results and comparison with experimental observations.

source: These observations could be consistent with compaction by cohesins performing one-sided loop extrusion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of simulation results with experimental observations.

source: In contrast, one-sided extrusion could account for some, but not all, of the observations of chromatin domains in yeast Hi-C, micro-C, and ChIA-PET experiments.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of simulation results with experimental observations.

claim: Yeast condensins compact pre- and post-rDNA genomic regions and mitotic chromosomes into insulated domains that do not exhibit the dots that are indicative of bringing boundaries together.
source: Yeast condensins compact pre- and post-rDNA genomic regions (in S. cerevisiae) (Lazar‐Stefanita et al., 2017; Schalbetter et al., 2017) and mitotic chromosomes (S. pombe) (Kakui et al., 2017; Tanizawa et al., 2017) into insulated domains that do not exhibit the dots that are indicative of bringing boundaries together.

source: In a similar manner, fission yeast cohesins organize small chromatin domains without dots (Kim et al., 2016; Mizuguchi et al., 2014; Tanizawa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

source: As shown in Figure 3b, pure one-sided loop extrusion can generate domains without dots.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 3b.

source: Nonetheless, recent observations of chromatin domains with dots under certain conditions in budding yeast challenge the viability of one-sided extrusion by both condensin and cohesin.
evidence: This is based on recent experimental observations.

source: In quiescent cells, condensins generate dots at the corners of small (10–60 kb), transcription-silencing domains in micro-C maps (Swygert et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

source: In exponentially growing cells arrested during mitosis, cohesins can also generate dots in S phase (Ohno et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

source: This observation suggests that budding yeast condensins and/or cohesins are either effectively two-sided loop extruders or loaded at specific sites because one-sided extrusion alone cannot generate dots (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations and simulation results.

claim: A mix of two-sided cohesins and one-sided condensins could generate dots as in micro-C/Hi-C experiments, while remaining consistent with single-molecule experiments.
source: However, a mix of two-sided cohesins and one-sided condensins (e.g., similar to Figure 3d, right panels) could generate dots as in micro-C/Hi-C experiments, while remaining consistent with single-molecule experiments.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the simulation results.

claim: Cohesin-dependent dots have also been observed at sites of convergent transcription in Hi-C maps when cohesin is overexpressed in G1.
source: Cohesin-dependent dots have also been observed at sites of convergent transcription in Hi-C maps when cohesin is overexpressed in G1 (Dauban et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: One-sided extrusion assisted by RNA polymerases that can push one side of an SMC complex could in principle generate effectively two-sided (but asymmetric) extrusion.
source: While such dots can be explained by two-sided extrusion, we also considered the possibility that one-sided extrusion assisted by RNA polymerases that can push one side of an SMC complex (Lengronne et al., 2004; Ocampo-Hafalla and Uhlmann, 2011). For one-sided extrusion, this effect could in principle generate effectively two-sided (but asymmetric) extrusion, where the slower extruding subunit moves at the speed of transcription (~1 kb/min).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the model and experimental observations.

claim: For typical cohesin residence times, this model suggests that small loops of 10–60 kb could be generated by the combined activity of loop extrusion and transcription.
source: For typical cohesin residence times (Gerlich et al., 2006b; Hansen et al., 2017; Kueng et al., 2006; Tedeschi et al., 2013; Wutz et al., 2017), this model suggests that small loops of 10–60 kb (Dauban et al., 2020; Ohno et al., 2019) could be generated by the combined activity of loop extrusion and transcription (Figure 3—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model and experimental measurements.

claim: One-sided extrusion by condensin and cohesin can reproduce some, but not all, of the chromosome organization phenomena observed in yeast.
source: In summary, one-sided extrusion by condensin and cohesin can reproduce some, but not all, of the chromosome organization phenomena observed in yeast.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of simulation results with experimental observations.

claim: The lower degree of mitotic chromosome compaction and formation of chromatin domains without dots is consistent with one-sided extrusion by yeast SMC complexes.
source: The lower degree of mitotic chromosome compaction (Guacci et al., 1994; Kruitwagen et al., 2018; Schalbetter et al., 2017) and formation of chromatin domains without dots (Kakui et al., 2017; Lazar‐Stefanita et al., 2017; Mizuguchi et al., 2014; Schalbetter et al., 2017; Tanizawa et al., 2017) is consistent with one-sided extrusion by yeast SMC complexes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of simulation results with experimental observations.

source: However, pure one-sided extrusion alone is insufficient to form dots in Hi-C and micro-C (Dauban et al., 2020; Ohno et al., 2019; Swygert et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of simulation results with experimental observations.

claim: Consistent with single-molecule experiments, budding yeast condensins could be one-sided, but then cohesins must be two-sided or effectively two-sided in order to generate Hi-C patterns in quiescent cells.
source: Consistent with single-molecule experiments, budding yeast condensins could be one-sided, but then cohesins must be two-sided or effectively two-sided in order to generate Hi-C patterns in quiescent cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of simulation results with experimental observations.

claim: In metaphase, budding yeast cohesins may be one-sided extruders, but their interphase activity during exponential growth requires two-sided or effectively two-sided extrusion.
source: In metaphase, budding yeast cohesins may be one-sided extruders, but their interphase activity during exponential growth requires two-sided or effectively two-sided extrusion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of simulation results with experimental observations.

claim: Our work identifies two requirements for loop extrusion by SMC complexes to generate known chromosome structures: unlooped chromatin gaps between SMC complexes must be closed, and extrusion must be two-sided or effectively two-sided.
source: Our work identifies two requirements for loop extrusion by SMC complexes to generate known chromosome structures. First, unlooped chromatin gaps between SMC complexes must be closed in order to compact mitotic chromosomes, and they occasionally must be closed between extrusion barriers during interphase to generate enrichment of CTCF-CTCF interactions. Second, particularly in prokaryotes, we find that extrusion must be two-sided or effectively two-sided in order to juxtapose bacterial chromosome arms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: Whether loop extrusion can compact and resolve chromosomes within physiological limits is a persistent question for chromosome organization in higher eukaryotes.
source: Whether loop extrusion can compact and resolve chromosomes within physiological limits is a persistent question for chromosome organization in higher eukaryotes.
evidence: This is a statement about an ongoing question in the field.

claim: Previous work on two-sided loop extrusion showed that LEFs can compact and resolve metazoan chromosomes (~100 Mb in length) for physiological densities of LEFs (1 per d = 10–30 kb).
source: Previous work on two-sided loop extrusion (Goloborodko et al., 2016a) showed that LEFs can compact and resolve metazoan chromosomes (~100 Mb in length) for physiological densities of LEFs (1 per d = 10–30 kb [Fukui and Uchiyama, 2007; Takemoto et al., 2004; Walther et al., 2018]).
evidence: This is based on previous modeling work and experimental measurements.

claim: Compaction and resolution are completed within a few (~5) residence times, provided that extrusion is fast, i.e., v > 0.2 kb/s.
source: Compaction and resolution are completed within a few (~5) residence times (1/kunbind ~ 2–10 min [Gerlich et al., 2006a; Terakawa et al., 2017; Walther et al., 2018]), provided that extrusion is fast, i.e., v > 0.2 kb/s (Goloborodko et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is based on previous modeling work and experimental measurements.

claim: The extrusion rate of v≈1 kb/s recently observed in vitro confirms that loop extrusion is sufficiently rapid to compact metazoan chromosomes during prophase and prometaphase.
source: The extrusion rate of v≈1 kb/s recently observed in vitro (Davidson et al., 2019; Ganji et al., 2018; Golfier et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2019; Kong et al., 2020) confirms that loop extrusion is sufficiently rapid to compact metazoan chromosomes during prophase and prometaphase.
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements and comparison with modeling predictions.

claim: This rate is consistent with expectations from studies of the molecular dynamics of loop-extruding SMC complexes.
source: Moreover, this rate is consistent with expectations from studies of the molecular dynamics of loop-extruding SMC complexes (Diebold-Durand et al., 2017; Marko et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on theoretical studies of SMC complex dynamics.

claim: The ATP cost to extrude 6 Gb is of order 10^8, which is less than the ~10^9 ATP present in the cell and less than the ~10^9 ATP/s that the cell produces.
source: Conservatively estimating that condensin or cohesin require two ATP per extrusion step and several attempts to traverse each nucleosome (~150 bp), the ATP cost to extrude 6 Gb is of order 10 x (6 × 109/150)~108 (we assume only ~5 attempts because in vitro extrusion speeds are not measurably altered by nucleosomes [Kim et al., 2019; Kong et al., 2020]). This upper limit estimate is still less than the ~109 ATP present in the cell (Traut, 1994) and less than the ~109 ATP/s that the cell produces (Flamholz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an estimate based on experimental measurements and known cellular ATP levels.

claim: There are only ~10^5 cohesins and condensins in each living cell.
source: Moreover, there are only ~105 cohesins (Cattoglio et al., 2019; Holzmann et al., 2019) and condensins (Fukui and Uchiyama, 2007; Takemoto et al., 2004; Walther et al., 2018) in each living cell
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements.

claim: Given an ATPase rate of ~1 s−1, the rate of actual energy consumption by loop extrusion is ~10^5 s−1, well within the cell's energy budget.
source: given an ATPase rate of ~1 s−1, we estimate that the rate of actual energy consumption by loop extrusion is ~105 s−1, well within the cell's energy budget.
evidence: This is an estimate based on experimental measurements and known cellular ATP production rates.

claim: Genome compaction and organization by loop extrusion is energetically feasible.
source: We conclude that genome compaction and organization by loop extrusion is energetically feasible.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the energy budget calculations.

claim: It has previously been suggested that 3D attractive interactions between LEFs could facilitate compaction of mitotic chromosomes.
source: It has previously been suggested that 3D attractive interactions between LEFs could facilitate compaction of mitotic chromosomes (Cheng et al., 2015; Sakai et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on previous theoretical work.

claim: For mitotic chromosomes, our results, along with previous work on polymer combs, suggests that 3D attractive interactions between LEFs cannot be the mechanism of chromatin gap closure.
source: For mitotic chromosomes, our results, along with previous work on polymer combs, suggests otherwise (Fytas and Theodorakis, 2013; Sheiko et al., 2004). It is possible that SMC complexes may attract each other, but such interactions must be weak enough that the chromosome does not collapse into a spherically symmetric polymer. With weak interactions, however, gaps created by one-sided extrusion cannot be closed, and mitotic chromosomes cannot be formed (Figure 2—figure supplement 5). Thus, 3D interactions cannot be the mechanism of chromatin gap closure, and thus, they cannot be essential for mitotic chromosome compaction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results and comparison with previous work on polymer physics.

claim: For interphase chromosomes, 3D attractions between TAD boundaries would not consistently pair CTCF boundaries in a convergent orientation nor would they distinguish between proximal and distal TAD boundaries.
source: For interphase chromosomes, 3D attractions between TAD boundaries (CTCF proteins or their binding sites) could potentially close chromatin gaps. However, 3D attractions would not consistently pair CTCF boundaries in a convergent orientation (Fudenberg et al., 2016; Sanborn et al., 2015) nor would they distinguish between proximal and distal TAD boundaries (Fudenberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the model mechanism and comparison with previous modeling work.

claim: For both mitotic and interphase chromosomes, attractive 3D interactions would promote trans interactions, contrasting with in vivo observations of condensin-mediated spatial resolution of mitotic chromosomes and cohesin-driven formation of cis loops.
source: Furthermore, for both mitotic and interphase chromosomes, attractive 3D interactions would promote trans interactions, contrasting with in vivo observations of condensin-mediated spatial resolution of mitotic chromosomes and cohesin-driven formation of cis loops.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the model mechanism and comparison with experimental observations.

claim: One-sided loop extrusion together with random cross-bridging of chromatin/DNA segments is not sufficient for compaction and domain formation.
source: All of these points suggest that one-sided loop extrusion together with random cross-bridging of chromatin/DNA segments as in several previous studies (Bohn and Heermann (2011); Bohn and Heermann (2010); Cheng et al. (2015)) is not sufficient for compaction and domain formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results and comparison with previous work.

claim: In simulations of mitotic chromosomes, alterations to LEF residence times due to LEF-LEF interactions do not enhance linear fold compaction.
source: In simulations of mitotic chromosomes, we found that alterations to LEF residence times due to LEF-LEF interactions do not enhance linear fold compaction (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
